doc.title: Tom Scott interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 1, 2022 [interview 1 of 2]

title: The studio soloist's job and the A&M complex in 1973
summary: He describes serving the artist, translating Joni Mitchell's colour language, and A&M as the centre of pop music.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: Okay. So now we’re talking about, we just transitioned nicely to those studio cats, which you of course it’s been a big part of your life. And your rise from let’s say second alto to soloist I guess was because you did well at every stage?
I guess. I mean life is a continuum and so it’s, yes. That must have been it.

Okay. So let’s say we’re going to pick — you had mentioned 1973 that there was a heck of a lot of things you did that year. And in that time period can you talk me through a typical day in the life of Tom Scott as far as perhaps getting a call to play a solo on someone’s record. Can you tell me how that happens and then what it was like in the studio?

You bet, sure. First of all your job if you’re playing a solo on someone else’s record obviously your job is to provide a service. You’re a gun for hire so to speak and your job is to make them happy with whatever you do. So I look to the artist and/or the producer to give me any input that they want to. Sometimes it’s in musical terms, many times it isn’t. You know they want it to feel some more emotion here or in the case of Joni Mitchell she was a painter you know, and still is a painter. So she would say I don’t know I want it more green over here. Now what the hell does that mean? Well it’s my job to translate into music. Because Joni and many of the people I worked with were not formally educated in music. They didn’t know how — Joni didn’t even know, with all those beautiful chords that she used to make up on the piano and the guitar, she couldn’t name one of them. She didn’t care what they were called. She just liked the sound of them. And so it was my job to figure out what it is that I can add to this thing to make it better than when I walked in. So ’73 I think in the very beginning of the year I did a tune with Carole King called “Jazzman.” And I had not yet met Carole King. I think I met Lou Adler. Because I used to work, as many of us studio musicians did, at A&M Recording complex, which formerly was the Charlie Chaplin Studio many years ago in the silent era, and currently I think it’s called the Jim Hensen Studio now. But there was a complex in the back of — one, two, three, four — four recording rooms and I used to be called to go in there all the time. And boy you could walk in there, it seemed like the center of the pop music universe back then because there’d be like Billy Preston over here and the Carpenters over here, and the Captain & Tenille, and John Lennon and Phil Spector in another room.
